stories.headline: Colorado launches common application to speed affordable housing funding
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis and Denver Mayor Mike Johnston announced Monday in Denver a standardized application for affordable housing developers seeking federal and state funding. The common application, set to launch in February, offers a single point of entry for financing ranging from tax credits to grants.

Officials said developers have had to navigate separate applications with as many as 189 questions, reproducing market studies, legal work, design information and financial projections. The state estimates the new process will cut costs by roughly $20,000 per unit and save up to four months of work. Laura Brudzynski, CEO of Lakewood-based Archway Communities, said the savings translate into more homes.

The application builds on Housing Hub Colorado, a website launched last year, and both grew out of the Colorado Housing Consortium. A 2023 state demography study estimated a deficit of 106,000 housing units, down from a 2019 peak of 140,000, and said Colorado must build about 34,100 homes a year over the next decade. The partnership includes the state, Denver and the Colorado Housing and Finance Authority.

stories.headline: Colorado treasurer candidates split over how state should invest billions
stories.summary:
The race for Colorado treasurer centers on how the next chief financial officer should manage the state's $15 billion to $20 billion investment portfolio, now concentrated in U.S. Treasury and mortgage bonds. Democratic state Sen. Jeff Bridges of Greenwood Village wants to redirect some funds to Colorado-specific projects such as renewable energy and affordable housing.

Republican Kevin Grantham, a former state Senate president and Fremont County commissioner, said the idea would expose the state to unnecessary risk. He argued the office should keep its longtime focus on safe, liquid investments free of political agendas. Libertarian Jodie Barr and Marilee Langner Sturgis of the Approval Voting Party are also on the Nov. 3 ballot.

The treasurer's office also returns unclaimed property and holds a seat on the Colorado PERA board. Bridges' idea is not unprecedented; a University of Colorado finance professor noted states including Ohio, Illinois and Vermont dedicate some treasury funds to in-state investments. The current treasurer, Dave Young, is term-limited.

stories.headline: Laubacher's money and moderate profile test Boebert in Colorado's 4th District
stories.summary:
Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, is challenging Republican U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert in the Nov. 3 election in the 4th Congressional District, the state's most Republican. The district spans 21 counties across the Eastern Plains and parts of the Front Range, and Republicans have nearly 100,000 more active registered voters than Democrats.

Laubacher, 58, became a Democrat only last year and has described herself as very moderate. She declined to endorse Melat Kiros, who defeated Rep. Diana DeGette in the June 1st District primary. She has raised more than 11 times what Boebert has.

Colorado State University political scientist Robert Duffy said Laubacher has the resume to win if the political climate favors Democrats. Boebert has clashed with President Donald Trump over the Epstein files and his veto of funding for a water pipeline in her district. The Cook Political Report recently outlined a more difficult path for Boebert.

stories.headline: Vigil and Haffley meet in rematch for Colorado Springs House District 16
stories.summary:
Democrat Stephanie Vigil is running against Republican Jill Haffley in Colorado House District 16, two years after losing the seat by three votes following a recount. Republican Rebecca Keltie won in 2024 in one of the closest margins in state history.

Haffley is a former teacher and member of the Colorado Springs School District 11 board. The district covers central Colorado Springs neighborhoods including Patty Jewett, Knob Hill and Papeton, and was expected to lean red after redistricting, though Vigil won it first.

Unaffiliated voters make up 52% of El Paso County, and Republican presidential candidates now win about 55% there rather than 60% or more. Local party figures disagree on whether the seat will keep flipping. Vigil said she plans to serve the full term allowed under term limits if elected.

stories.headline: Denver archbishop says he is 'heartbroken' by reaction to White House prayer
stories.summary:
Denver Archbishop James Golka said his participation in a prayer over President Donald Trump in the Oval Office was not meant as an endorsement. He spoke to the Denver Catholic after the White House released video of the Thursday event, 12 days before the Nov. 3 elections.

Golka said he and other bishops met administration officials to discuss immigration, including visas for religious workers, as well as protection of life, religious freedom and school choice. He acknowledged he knew people might be upset and that the event could be used politically.

CNN reported two other bishops regretted attending, and Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob apologized publicly. Golka became Denver's archbishop earlier this year after serving as bishop in Colorado Springs, succeeding Samuel Aquila.

stories.headline: Developers sue Broomfield over permit requirements for $300M Town Square project
stories.summary:
The Broomfield Town Square Alliance has sued the city of Broomfield over permit requirements tied to a $300 million downtown development, according to the Denver Business Journal.

The lawsuit challenges conditions the city has placed on the project's permits. The development is a major planned investment in Broomfield's downtown.

The Business Journal also reported that Denver-based oil company Ovintiv is buying Canadian company Logan Energy Corp., which holds assets in the Montney Basin.

stories.headline: Third Denver Trader Joe's to open in Central Park in 2027
stories.summary:
Trader Joe's will open a new Denver store in 2027 at 8564 E. Northfield Blvd. in the Central Park neighborhood, near the Avenues at Northfield mall. No opening date has been set.

The chain has nine stores across eight Colorado cities. The new location will be Denver's third, after stores on North Colorado Boulevard and Logan Street.

Trader Joe's also announced in 2025 plans for a ground-floor space in a five-story apartment building in Platt Park, to be developed by Kentro Group. That project was still under city review Monday, though the chain has been approved for a liquor license at 567 E. Louisiana Ave.

stories.headline: Golden restaurateur closes Nosu Ramen and Abejas Bistro
stories.summary:
Two longtime Golden restaurants have closed. Nosu Ramen, at 700 12th St. since 2020, announced its closure at the beginning of October, and its sister restaurant Abejas Bistro, at 807 13th St. for 11 years, closed permanently days later.

Co-owner Brandon Bortles said Nosu's lease was up after six years. He cited rising operating costs, changing economic conditions and financial pressures that made a lease extension unsustainable.

Abejas had first been described as temporarily closed because of ongoing building issues. Its owners said the restaurant industry has changed considerably in recent years.

stories.headline: Golf-themed coworking space Clubhouse Work & Golf expands to Colorado Boulevard
stories.summary:
Clubhouse Work & Golf is opening a second location in the Galleria Towers at 720 S. Colorado Blvd., near Cherry Creek, after its Greenwood Village site proved popular. The space spans 23,000 square feet on two floors with 65 private offices, shared areas, conference rooms and five golf simulators.

Memberships start at $300 a month for social memberships and range to private offices at $1,100 a month and up. The Greenwood Village location is also adding 30 offices.

Elsewhere, Warby Parker opened its seventh Colorado store at Flatiron Crossing. BOXBOX leased space at 3003 E. 3rd Ave. in Cherry Creek, with an expanded menu expected in early 2027.

stories.headline: Broncos defense improves tackling ahead of Sunday's game against Chiefs
stories.summary:
The Broncos (5-2) host Kansas City (5-1) Sunday at Empower Field, and their defense has cut down on the missed tackles that plagued a 31-10 Week 1 loss at Arrowhead. In that game the Broncos missed 24 tackles and Kansas City ran for 220 yards.

Since then Denver has missed 30 tackles in six games, about five per game, and is allowing 118.8 rushing yards per game. The Broncos held Arizona to 94 rushing yards Sunday.

Former Broncos Louis Wright and Karl Mecklenburg noted the improvement. Kenneth Walker III, who ran for 173 yards against Denver in Week 1, had 36 yards for Seattle in Week 7.

stories.headline: Colorado avalanche forecasts begin as investigators detail how accident reviews save lives
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche Information Center will begin issuing daily forecasts for the winter season Sunday. When an avalanche involves people, the center reconstructs what happened, examines contributing factors and identifies lessons for backcountry users.

Deputy director Brian Lazar said his approach changed after a 2011 death on Torreys Peak, when showing the skier's family photographs helped them understand the accident. Early reports simply recorded facts, while today's investigators use a standardized format that explains decisions in context.

A skier was partially buried Sunday on Mount Bross in the season's first recorded avalanche and was rescued by companions, the center said.

topStory.headline: Source Material Does Not Cover Reported Poll on Democratic Midterm Gains; Article Provided Is on Vehicle Dashboard Warning Lights
topStory.summary:
The topic assigned for this summary is a poll showing Democrats still poised to make gains, with warning signs about how large those gains may be. However, the only source supplied, a piece from nationalheraldindia.com, contains no reporting on that subject. The article is a consumer guide explaining dashboard warning lights in modern vehicles, and it is also cut off mid-sentence at a section on the battery warning.

The article describes how dashboard indicators connect to a vehicle's monitoring and diagnostic systems and use colors to signal severity, though meanings can vary by manufacturer and model. It covers the check engine light, which can point to a faulty sensor, ignition problems, emission system issues, or fuel system irregularities. A steady light calls for professional diagnosis, while a flashing light can signal a more serious problem needing immediate attention.

The guide also addresses the oil pressure warning, shown as an oil-can symbol, which indicates insufficient lubrication and can cause severe engine damage if ignored. Drivers are advised to stop safely, switch off the engine, and seek professional help. The engine temperature warning, shown as a thermometer amid waves, signals overheating from causes such as low coolant, radiator problems, or fan failure, and drivers are warned not to open a hot radiator cap because pressurized coolant can cause serious burns.

Because the source material has no information on the poll, the parties involved, polling figures, the political context, or upcoming electoral events, a factual summary of the Democratic gains story cannot be written from it. Details such as who conducted the poll, the margins reported, and the specific warning signs for Democrats would need to come from a relevant source. A correct article or the poll's original reporting should be supplied before this item is published.
